Three bizarre stories caught my eye this weekend, all insane and all pointing
to the same thing: national security's war on American daily life.

  1. **Flock cameras**. The AI-fueled license plate reading network is conquering America at an alarming pace, having found an ingenious end-run around our right to privacy: selling to the neighbors instead of the cops.

  2. **ICE is acquiring robot dogs.** The most hated agency in America is shopping for Boston Dynamics quadrupeds to take another bite out of the quaint notion that this country isn't a battlefield.

  3. **WNBA embraces Counterterrorism.** The WNBA team Chicago Sky is in the news this month for hiring a threat intelligence firm -- one built to fight ISIS -- to respond to a supposed "extremist" menace to its players.

National security has colonized American culture so completely that none of
this registers as creepy. Flock cameras become a cranky privacy controversy.
ICE's robo-dogs become a zany story you roll your eyes at. A counterterrorism
firm for basketball players becomes a friendly [write-
up](https://www.npr.org/2026/08/29/nx-s1-5947897/wnba-national-security) on
NPR about the importance of combating extremism in sports.

Flock Safety, whose AI-powered license plate readers now sit on poles in
thousands of American towns, has become the poster child for the surveillance
state. But the state is only half the problem. The other half of Flock's
revenue comes from private clients: homeowners associations, apartment
complexes, strip-mall owners.

The Fourth Amendment restrains the government. It has nothing to say about
your HOA -- and there is no fascist entity in America more powerful than the
HOA. So through no fault of your own, your vehicle's make, model, and driver
get fed continuously into a massive database of movements.

ICE, meanwhile, is buying Boston Dynamics' quadrupedal (four-legged, sheesh)
robot dogs for "public safety," on the solemn theory that the danger to its
agents has grown too grave to face on two legs. Strip away the breathless talk
and one stubborn fact remains: not a single ICE agent was killed in the line
of duty this past year. Not one. Yet to hear the agency tell it, there's an
epidemic.

Perhaps ICE should examine its own behavior and leash itself.

The WNBA story is stranger still: a basketball team retaining a national
security threat intelligence firm to counter a supposed "extremist" threat.
Pointing to the rivalry between Angel Reese and Caitlin Clark, NPR laments the
online threats and abuse directed at Reese, then hands the ball to Moonshot --
an outfit founded to disrupt ISIS recruitment and the spread of jihadism
online.

Working with Google's tech incubator Jigsaw, Moonshot built the "Redirect
Method" during the war on terror: algorithmic search-ad targeting that steered
people looking for terrorist propaganda toward curated de-radicalization
content. It is the height of naivete to think a man drawn to violent jihad can
be search-added into the Boy Scouts. But that is now the methodology being
deployed against people who are rude about basketball on the internet.

As Elizabeth Neumann, Moonshot's chief strategy officer, told NPR:

> "It says a lot that here we are, 10 years later, taking that same
> technology, the methodologies that we use to help governments counter
> terrorism and other targeted violence, and we are now having to apply it to
> sports entertainment,"

It does say a lot -- though not in the sense that she means.

Neumann personifies the revolving door between the federal homeland security
apparatus and the private threat-monitoring industry. She served in government
national security roles from the Bush to Trump administrations, most recently
as Assistant Secretary for Counterterrorism and Threat Prevention at the
Department of Homeland Security before entering the private counter-extremism
consulting world.

Treating social media hostility (a redundancy if ever there was one!) as a
national security contingency requiring counter-extremism methodologies is
institutional mission creep at its finest. Internet vitriol is real and nasty
-- sometimes even justifying a law enforcement response. But to frame that
vitriol as a problem of radicalization elevates the problem to the domain of
national security, which treats the problem as something akin to an
insurgency.

This brings us back to Flock Safety. The genius of modern surveillance is that
it doesn't require an authoritarian decree from Washington to carpet the
country in a movement tracking system. It just needs bottom-up panic, which of
course national security and its corporate adjuncts happily create.

When Flock launched, it didn't start by grinding through municipal red tape,
contentious city council votes, or public procurement debates. It pitched
directly to suburban HOA boards. By selling automated vehicle tracking to
neighborhood Karens who monitor their cul-de-sacs with more vigilance than the
Pentagon does the Strait of Hormuz, Flock bypassed the very ideals that make
America, America in the first place.

Local police departments then partner with the HOAs, gaining real-time access
to a sprawling, privately financed surveillance dragnet that taxpayers never
had to approve. Then the network of cameras expands, you know, to respond to
Amber alerts, and then to kids on electric bikes, and then pretty soon,
through the wonders of AI, the entire country is ruled by the big HOA on the
lamppost.

This is what permanent war looks like when it comes home.

Rather than a rogue CIA or FBI, it looks like a culture that has come to
believe everyday life demands constant threat modeling, automated
surveillance, and counterinsurgency. The mainstream media meanwhile misses the
point, at best trotting out some civil liberties expert who puts you to sleep
with an undergraduate seminar on the Fourth Amendment.

In my own reporting, I've moved away from the term "national security state"
because it's not just a government phenomenon. Now I just say "national
security."
